shared_context.patient: A 26-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a 6-month history of increasing lower back pain. He first felt the pain while lifting boxes at work but thought that he had just strained a muscle. The pain appears to be worse in the mornings and after rest. Exercise and physical activity appear to temporarily make the pain better. He has taken acetaminophen and ibuprofen for the pain. He has no significant medical history and takes no medications. His temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure is 115/70 mmHg, pulse is 70/min, and respirations are 12/min. On physical exam, he is found to have limited flexion and extension of his spine as well as tenderness to palpation over the insertion of his patellar tendons bilaterally. Results from laboratory tests are shown below: Serum: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 61 mm/hr C-reactive protein (CRP): 36 mg/L (normal <10 mg/L)

atoms.1: Symptoms that worsen in the mornings and after rest, and improve with exercise and physical activity are characteristic of inflammatory back pain.
atoms.2: Elevation in ESR and CRP levels suggests an underlying inflammatory process.
atoms.3: Limited flexion and extension of the spine, as well as tenderness to palpation over the insertion of the patellar tendons bilaterally, suggest spondyloarthritis.
atoms.4: The patient's condition is particularly suggestive of ankylosing spondylitis.
atoms.5: In spondyloarthritis, plain radiographs (X-rays) can show changes in the spine.
atoms.6: In spondyloarthritis, plain radiographs (X-rays) can show changes in the sacroiliac joints.
atoms.7: Changes in the spine and sacroiliac joints may not be visible in the early stages of spondyloarthritis.
atoms.8: Bone scans are not generally used for diagnosing spondyloarthritis.
atoms.9: Bone scans are more often used for detecting bone metastasis.
atoms.10: Bone scans are more often used for detecting osteomyelitis.
atoms.11: Computed tomography (CT) scans provide more detailed images than X-rays.
atoms.12: CT scans can help identify sacroiliitis.
atoms.13: CT scans can help identify spinal changes in more detail.
atoms.14: MRI provides the most sensitive detection of early changes in spondyloarthritis.
atoms.15: MRI is the preferred imaging modality for diagnosing spondyloarthritis.
atoms.16: Ultrasound is not typically used for initial imaging of spondyloarthritis.
atoms.17: The most accurate test for the patient's condition is Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI).

snippets.output: Symptoms that worsen in the mornings and after rest, and improve with exercise and physical activity are characteristic of inflammatory back pain.
Elevation in ESR and CRP levels suggests an underlying inflammatory process.

Limited flexion and extension of the spine as well as tenderness to palpation over the insertion of the patellar tendons bilaterally, this is suggestive of spondyloarthritis (SpA), particularly ankylosing spondylitis.
